common_name: Church Mouse Hosta (Variegated Mini Blue Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions or potted starts in spring or early fall into humus-rich, well-drained shade soil; this slow-growing sport takes a couple of seasons to bulk up to a full clump.

directions: Grow in consistently moist, well-drained soil in dappled to deep shade, sheltered from hot afternoon sun which can scorch the thin variegated margin. This is a creamy-white-margined sport of 'Blue Mouse Ears' with the same thick, rounded, cupped blue-green leaves, forming a dense low mound. Slug and snail control is important since the small stature makes damage disproportionately noticeable. Divide congested clumps in early spring or fall to increase stock; it is slower to multiply than many mini hostas.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder - Hosta

planting.note: Set divisions in spring or early fall in rich, evenly moist soil with good drainage; give it room to cascade over an edge or slope for best visual effect.

directions: Grow in partial to full shade in soil that stays evenly moist but drains well; morning sun is tolerated in cooler climates but hot afternoon exposure fades the streaking. Narrow, wavy-margined leaves with irregular white-to-cream streaking down a green background give this cultivar a flowing, cascading habit, making it well suited to raised beds, slopes, or container edges. Watch for slug damage on the thin leaf blades and apply an organic mulch to conserve moisture and suppress weeds. Because it is a streaked sport, occasional reversion shoots (solid green) should be cut out at the base to keep the pattern stable.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich soil; give it several seasons to reach full mature height and flowering size.

directions: Grow in part to full shade with consistently moist, fertile, well-drained soil; this cultivar wilts quickly if it dries out and appreciates a cool root run and mulch. Deeply cut, near-black purple foliage forms a handsome mound through summer, then in late summer to early fall tall, dark, wiry stems send up fragrant white bottlebrush flower spikes that are excellent for late-season pollinators. Site it out of strong wind since the tall flower stems can topple in exposed spots, and avoid hot afternoon sun which bleaches the dark foliage color. Established clumps resent disturbance, so divide only when necessary and water in well afterward.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder - Actaea simplex

common_name: Fire Dragon Persicaria (Painter's Palette Selection with Maroon Chevron)

planting.note: Plant divisions or potted starts in spring into moist, humus-rich shade soil; site with some room since it self-sows and spreads readily once established.

directions: Grow in part to full shade in moist, organically rich soil; unlike the plain species this selection holds its bold maroon-red V-shaped leaf chevron best with some protection from hot midday sun. Thin wiry stems carry small red-tinted flower spikes in late summer into fall that mature into red-brown jumping seed capsules. It self-sows freely and can naturalize into a substantial patch in a woodland setting, so remove spent flower stalks before seed drop if a tighter clump is preferred. Cut back tattered foliage in late fall; new growth emerges reliably from the crown each spring.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox - Persicaria virginiana
